summary:
Nothing in Honduran law criminalises a person's gender identity. The Penal Code, amended by Decree No. 23-2013 and in force since March 2017, treats hatred or contempt based on sexual orientation or gender identity as an aggravating circumstance in criminal responsibility (Article 27); punishes anyone who arbitrarily blocks, restricts or denies individual or collective rights, or refuses a professional service, on those grounds with three to five years' imprisonment and a fine of four to seven minimum wages (Article 321); and punishes public or media incitement to discrimination, hatred or violence against a person or group on listed grounds including sexual orientation and gender identity with three to five years' imprisonment and fines of L.50,000 to L.300,000 (Article 321-A). LGBTI rights groups met Congress during the reform process to press for the wording of Articles 321 and 321-A to be retained, and the anti-discrimination provisions were kept. A name change for LGBTI persons is approved in Honduras.

The enforcement picture is severe. Honduras has one of the world's highest rates of violence against women and LGBTI persons, and trans women face the greatest obstacles to obtaining justice. The LAWG Education Fund attributes the resulting impunity to under-reporting, a lack of police and prosecutor training, insufficient resources, and the intentional mishandling of cases, concluding that the institutions fail to effectively investigate and prosecute. The US State Department's 2021 Human Rights Report for Honduras lists violence and threats against LGBTQI+ persons, extrajudicial killings, torture, corruption and lack of accountability for gender-based violence among the country's significant human rights issues. Human Rights Watch finds that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide legal frameworks, with officials in the region describing them as not biological women; Vicky Hernandez v Honduras, heard at the Inter-American Court of Human Rights, is the leading transfemicide case.

Police conduct carries specific risk for trans visitors and residents. Human Rights Watch's May 2009 report, Not Worth a Penny, documents police rape, assault and extortion of transgender people in Honduras. The 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs permits police to raid streets, entrap sex workers under sanitation control, and arrest anyone who goes against modesty, proper conduct and public morals; LGBTQ organisations document repeated use of that provision as a pretext to harass and detain transgender women, restricting their access to public space. Early LGBTQ organisations also faced police harassment despite formal association rights under the Constitution, and initial attempts to register an LGBTQ rights group in the 1980s met government opposition or extended delays.

Detention is a documented danger. Transgender women are held in the men's prison system. At Penitenciaria Nacional Tamara, LGBTI prisoners are concentrated in the La Isla module beside the mentally ill unit; trans women are forced to cut their hair, barred from presenting as women, and denied conjugal visits, with guards stating that they are men. At Penitenciaria de Marcala authorities seized a trans woman's clothes and cut her hair, and only after intervention by the torture-prevention centre CPTRT was she isolated from male prisoners and her belongings returned. Placement follows birth sex with de facto LGBTI grouping and ad hoc protective isolation, and there is no placement-by-gender-identity policy. Human Rights Watch reported in October 2020 that Honduras places transgender women in men's prisons, which can lead to physical and sexual abuse; a Honduran judge described a case in which a trans woman was raped by fellow detainees with the complicity of prison guards, told prosecutors, and saw no investigation, stating that there is no way to protect trans women in men's prisons.

Partner and family recognition is barred. The 2005 constitutional amendment expressly prohibits same-sex marriage and de facto unions, refuses to recognise same-sex marriages or unions performed lawfully abroad (Article 112), and bars same-sex couples from adopting (Article 116); same-sex couples and same-sex-headed households are ineligible for the legal protections available to opposite-sex married couples.

Trans visibility has grown alongside the security costs attached to it. A trans activist and co-founder of Asociacion Cozumel Trans ran for Congress in Francisco Morazan for the PINU party at the 26 November 2017 election, potentially becoming the first openly trans officeholder; she had won her party primary earlier that year, and Claudia Spellman had run for the LIBRE party in 2012. Victoria Gomez sought asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa. About 400 people marched in a pride parade in San Pedro Sula in July 2017.

Public services are offered without formal exclusion but are constrained in practice. The government provides medical care to all citizens and has worked increasingly with non-governmental organisations on HIV/AIDS awareness, yet the influence of the Catholic Church and evangelical Protestant churches has made comprehensive public programmes difficult to implement, and no youth-specific care or medication provisions appear. Police harassment and political hostility remain live factors: the two major parties have largely ignored LGBTQ rights, three candidates who backed same-sex marriage before the November 2017 elections all failed to win National Congress seats, President Juan Orlando Hernández stated on 12 October 2018 that as a Christian he opposes same-sex marriage, and the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association has urged President Xiomara Castro to stop immoral laws.
tangentialFactors:
The regional pattern matters for context. Human Rights Watch's finding that Central American states exclude transgender women from femicide frameworks indicates that the gap in Honduran law is shared with neighbouring jurisdictions, and the leading regional transfemicide case is brought against Honduras itself. The LAWG Education Fund places Honduras alongside El Salvador among the world's highest-rate countries for violence against women and LGBTI persons.

Religious institutional opposition is a persistent current. Organised protests by the Catholic Church, Pentecostal groups and conservative legislators accompanied the 2004 government decision to extend formal recognition to three LGBTQ rights interest groups, and church leaders have publicly attacked both same-sex unions and the approved name-change procedure, with the president of the Tegucigalpa Pastors' Association calling it an aberration in God's eyes.

The violence timeline is documented across several decades. A dated GlobalGayz archive of Honduran LGBT news from 2004 to 2011 records an August 2004 church protest at state recognition of three gay groups, 2009 and 2010 items on an LGBT activist murdered amid violence and impunity, extreme violence against the gay community and abuses after the 2009 coup, and 2005 coverage of marriage and adoption bans. These are archive excerpts rather than primary reporting, so they corroborate the timeline without independently establishing case details.
localsOnly:
Association rights are constitutionally available, but LGBTQ groups historically obtained recognition only after delay or opposition, and the first organisations arose in response to the HIV/AIDS pandemic with no legal standing and effectively no government engagement beyond police harassment.

Political participation by openly trans people has been attempted repeatedly: Claudia Spellman ran for the LIBRE party in 2012, Kendra Stefani Jordany won a PINU primary in 2017, and the same party's general-election congressional candidacy in Francisco Morazan on 26 November 2017 was potentially the first openly trans run for office. Victoria Gomez left for asylum in Spain after threats and attacks in Tegucigalpa.

Residents are exposed to police powers under the 2001 Law on Police and Social Affairs, which authorises sanitation-control entrapment and arrest for conduct deemed against modesty, proper conduct and public morals. LGBTQ organisations document its use against transgender women as a routine limit on street presence.

Prison conditions for trans women are governed by birth-sex placement. Corresponsales Clave reporting of 6 September 2017, drawing on CPTRT, records forced haircuts, confiscation of feminine clothing, denial of conjugal visits and de facto concentration in the La Isla module at Tamara, with protective isolation arranged case by case and no policy based on gender identity.

HIV/AIDS prevention work continues through partnerships with non-governmental organisations, with female prostitutes and men who sex with men identified as the highest-risk groups, and broader public programmes constrained by church influence.
outOfScopeNotes:
A Reuters feature on Central American LGBT people fleeing for their lives returned HTTP 401 and could not be retrieved at research time, so none of its specific claims are carried here; the underlying phenomenon is supported by the asylum case of Victoria Gomez in the Washington Blade reporting.

No procedure details are given for how an LGBTI person obtains a name change in Honduras, beyond the fact that it is approved and that church leaders have attacked it; the documentary requirements, processing time and whether the change extends to a passport or national identity card are unresolved.

No youth-specific care or medication provisions appear in the sources reviewed; whether gender-affirming healthcare is available, restricted or publicly funded is not sourced either way.

The 2017 congressional candidacy is described as potentially the first openly trans officeholder, and the sources do not confirm whether she won; the outcome of that election is unresolved here.

Case-level outcomes for the killings of LGBTI activists referenced in the GlobalGayz archive, and the current enforcement record for Articles 321 and 321-A since March 2017, are not sourced in this inventory.
